sections.h2: How does foreclosure work in Georgia?
sections.html:
Georgia is a non-judicial foreclosure state, so a lender holding a deed to secure debt can sell the home at auction without suing the borrower or appearing before a judge. The Attorney General's mortgage page points to O.C.G.A. 44-14-162 through 44-14-162.4 for the procedure.

Two papers sit behind the process. The promissory note is the borrower's promise to repay, and the deed to secure debt, which most people call the mortgage, gives the lender the legal right to take the house if the note goes unpaid. A default is usually missed payments, though the Attorney General notes it can also be a lapse in property insurance or unpaid property taxes.

sections.h2: What notice does a Georgia borrower get before the sale?
sections.html:
The borrower must be sent written notice at least 30 days before the proposed sale date, by registered or certified mail or statutory overnight delivery with return receipt, and the notice must carry a copy of the sale advertisement. It also has to name a person or entity with authority to negotiate, amend and modify the loan, with an address and telephone number.

Refusing a certified letter does not cancel the notice. The lender must also run the sale advertisement in the county's official legal newspaper once a week for four consecutive weeks, and if it has not already done so it must file proof of its ownership of the security instrument, usually an assignment, with the superior court clerk before the sale starts. That filing is one way a borrower can find out who holds the loan now.

sections.h2: When and where are Georgia foreclosure sales held?
sections.html:
Sales happen on the courthouse steps of the county where the property sits, on the first Tuesday of the month between 10:00 a.m. and 4:00 p.m. The Attorney General's consumer page adds that when the first Tuesday is a holiday the sale moves to the first Wednesday.

Bidding is open to the public, but the lender is frequently the only bidder. The lender signs a deed of foreclosure to the winning bidder, which may be the lender itself, and at that point the winner becomes the owner.

sections.h2: What can a homeowner do before the sale date?
sections.html:
Atlanta Legal Aid lists six ways a scheduled sale can be stopped, and each one should be confirmed in writing from the lender. A borrower who reaches an agreement should insist on a written confirmation that the sale is cancelled.

  • Reinstate the loan by paying the missed payments, attorney fees and foreclosure costs
  • Agree to a payment plan or loan modification
  • Sell the home and pay the mortgage off in full before the scheduled sale
  • Complete a short sale or deed in lieu of foreclosure, which the lender must approve
  • File bankruptcy before the sale, which stays a non-judicial foreclosure
  • Win a temporary restraining order by showing a legal basis, such as a notice defect

The Attorney General cautions that applying for a modification may not stop a sale, since homes have been sold while an application was still pending. Active duty service members may have extra protection under the federal Servicemembers Civil Relief Act.

sections.h2: Can I sell my Georgia house before the foreclosure sale?
sections.html:
Yes, a sale that pays the loan in full before the scheduled date is one of the options on the legal aid flyer, and it keeps the foreclosure off the table. Sellers who owe more than the house will bring should know that a short sale needs lender approval and can carry tax or deficiency consequences, so ask a lawyer or HUD certified housing counselor before agreeing.

A seller pays the state real estate transfer tax unless the contract says otherwise. The Superior Court Clerks' Cooperative Authority prints the rate as $1 for the first $1,000 and 10 cents for each additional $100 or fractional part of $100, due before the deed can be recorded. The Census Bureau counts 65.7 percent of Georgia homes as owner occupied for 2020 to 2024, and median monthly owner costs with a mortgage at $1,783.

sections.h2: What happens to the borrower after the foreclosure sale?
sections.html:
A valid foreclosure ends the borrower's right to live in the house, and the new owner can file a dispossessory action if the former owner stays. Legal aid describes the sequence: a demand to leave, a warrant that may be posted on the door, seven days to answer, a hearing about a week later, and seven days to move once a judge rules against the occupant.

Some buyers offer cash for keys in exchange for leaving the home empty and broom clean by a set date. In most cases the lender accepts the property as payment and the matter ends. The lender may instead sue for the gap between the sale price and the loan balance, which is called a deficiency proceeding and goes before the courts. Anyone who suspects a wrongful foreclosure should seek an attorney or legal aid quickly, and Atlanta Legal Aid's Home Defense Program can be reached at (770) 817-7538.

Watch for rescue scams. Legal aid warns about offers that take upfront fees, trick owners into signing over title, or promise that recording a document in the deed records will halt a sale. The Attorney General's page also warns against signing over a deed to save a home and against sending mortgage payments to anyone other than the holder.

faqs.q: How much notice does a Georgia lender have to give before foreclosing?
faqs.a: At least 30 days in writing before the proposed sale date. The notice goes by registered or certified mail or statutory overnight delivery, and it must include a copy of the sale advertisement and contact details for someone with authority to modify the loan.

faqs.q: What day are foreclosure sales held in Georgia?
faqs.a: The first Tuesday of each month, between 10:00 a.m. and 4:00 p.m., on the courthouse steps of the county where the home sits. The Attorney General's consumer page says a holiday moves the sale to the first Wednesday.

faqs.q: Does Georgia require a court case to foreclose?
faqs.a: No. Georgia is a non-judicial foreclosure state, and a lender can use the power of sale in the deed to secure debt without filing suit. A borrower who believes the process was flawed can go to court, for example to seek a restraining order.

faqs.q: Can a lender still sue me after the house is sold at foreclosure?
faqs.a: Yes, for any shortfall. The Attorney General's page says the holder may sue for the difference between the foreclosure price and what was owed on the note, called a deficiency proceeding. In most cases the lender simply keeps the property as satisfaction of the loan.

faqs.q: Will filing bankruptcy stop a Georgia foreclosure sale?
faqs.a: A properly filed bankruptcy petition stays a non-judicial foreclosure if it reaches the bankruptcy clerk before the property is sold. The lender may ask the bankruptcy judge for permission to resume, and the owner must keep paying the mortgage to keep the house. Talk to an attorney first because the filing has lasting effects.
